column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 31: “Be detached from this world”

column2: From Sahl ibn Saʿd al-Sāʿidī, who said: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said:

Messenger of Allah, direct me to a deed which, if I do it, Allah will love me and people will love me. He said: “Be detached from this world and Allah will love you; and be detached from what people possess and people will love you.”
A ḥasan hadith, reported by Ibn Mājah and others with ḥasan chains.

This hadith was recorded by Ibn Mājah through the narration of Khālid ibn ʿAmr al-Qurashī, from Sufyān al-Thawrī, from Abū Ḥāzim, from Sahl ibn Saʿd. The Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) stated that its chain is ḥasan, but that is open to question,

for of Khālid ibn ʿAmr al-Qurashī al-Umawī Imam Aḥmad said: His hadith is munkar; and he said once: He is not trustworthy; he narrates false hadiths. Ibn Maʿīn said: His hadith is worth nothing; and he said once: He was a liar who lied; he narrated fabricated hadiths from Shuʿbah.

Al-Bukhārī and Abū Zurʿah said: His hadith is munkar. Abū Ḥātim said: His hadith is abandoned (matrūk); he is weak. Ṣāliḥ ibn Muḥammad and Ibn ʿAdī attributed the fabrication of hadith to him. Ibn Ḥibbān contradicted himself about him, mentioning him both in Kitāb al-Thiqāt and in Kitāb al-Ḍuʿafāʾ,

where he said: He used to narrate fabrications from trustworthy narrators that no one else had; it is not permitted to cite his reports as proof. Al-ʿUqaylī recorded this hadith of his and said: It has no basis in the hadith of Sufyān al-Thawrī. He said: Muḥammad ibn Kathīr al-Ṣanʿānī corroborated Khālid in it; perhaps he took it from him and concealed the fact (tadlīs),
because the one known for it is this Khālid.
Abū Bakr al-Khaṭīb said: Abū Qatādah al-Ḥarrānī and Mihrān ibn Abī ʿUmar al-Rāzī also corroborated him, reporting it from al-Thawrī. He said: The best known of them is the hadith of Ibn Kathīr.

So he said; but this differs from al-ʿUqaylī's statement that the best known of them is the hadith of Khālid ibn ʿAmr, which is the more correct. Muḥammad ibn Kathīr al-Ṣanʿānī is al-Miṣṣīṣī; Aḥmad declared him weak.
Abū Qatādah and Mihrān have also been criticised; but Muḥammad ibn Kathīr is better than both of them, for he is trustworthy in the view of many of the ḥuffāẓ.
Ibn ʿAdī was astonished at this hadith of his and said: I do not know what to say about it.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim mentioned that he asked his father about the hadith of Muḥammad ibn Kathīr from Sufyān al-Thawrī, naming this hadith, and he said: This is a false hadith — meaning with this chain. He was indicating that it has no basis from Muḥammad ibn Kathīr from Sufyān.
Ibn Mushaysh said: I asked Aḥmad about the hadith of Sahl ibn Saʿd, and mentioned this hadith. Aḥmad said: Lā ilāha illā Allāh! — in astonishment at it — Who narrates this?

I said: Khālid ibn ʿAmr. He said: So we have landed on Khālid ibn ʿAmr! — and then fell silent. He meant to rebuke whoever mentioned to him anything of this Khālid's hadith, for it is not worth attending to.

Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām recorded it in his Kitāb al-Mawāʿiẓ from Khālid ibn ʿAmr, and then said: I used to reject this hadith, but this shaykh told me that Wakīʿ had asked him about it; were it not for this statement of his, I would have left it out.
Ibn ʿAdī recorded this hadith in his entry on Khālid ibn ʿAmr, mentioned Muḥammad ibn Kathīr's narration of it as well, and said: This hadith from al-Thawrī is munkar.
He said: Zāfir — meaning Ibn Sulaymān — reported it from Muḥammad ibn ʿUyaynah, Sufyān's brother, from Abū Ḥāzim, from Ibn ʿUmar.
End of quotation. Zāfir and Muḥammad ibn ʿUyaynah are both weak.

This hadith has also been narrated by another route, in mursal form. Abū Sulaymān ibn Zabr al-Dimashqī recorded it in the Musnad of Ibrāhīm ibn Adham that he compiled, through the narration of Muʿāwiyah ibn Ḥafṣ,
from Ibrāhīm ibn Adham, from Manṣūr, from Ribʿī ibn Ḥirāsh, who said:
A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: Messenger of Allah, direct me to a deed for which Allah will love me and people will love me.

He said: “As for the deed for which Allah will love you, it is detachment from this world; and as for the deed for which people will love you, look at this debris [of worldly goods] and throw it to them.”
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded it in Kitāb Dhamm al-Dunyā (“The Censure of This World”) through the narration of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, from Ibrāhīm ibn Adham, who said:
A man came to the Prophet ﷺ — and he related it, without mentioning Manṣūr or Ribʿī in its chain — and in his version he said: “Throw to them the debris that is in your hands.”
This hadith contains two great pieces of counsel.
The first is detachment from this world (zuhd), and that it brings about Allah's love for His servant.
The second is detachment from what people possess, and that it brings about people's love.

As for detachment from this world, there are many indications in the Qurʾān praising it and censuring desire for this world. The Exalted says: “But you prefer the life of this world, though the Hereafter is better and more lasting” [al-Aʿlā 87:16–17]; and: “You desire the goods of this world, but Allah desires the Hereafter” [al-Anfāl 8:67]; and the Exalted says in the story of Qārūn:

“So he went out before his people in his finery. Those who desired the life of this world said: If only we had the like of what Qārūn has been given; he is truly one of great fortune. But those who had been given knowledge said: Woe to you! Allah's reward is better for one who believes and does righteous deeds, and none attains it but the patient” [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:79–80] — up to His words:

“That is the abode of the Hereafter: We assign it to those who seek neither exaltation in the land nor corruption; and the end belongs to the God-fearing” [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:83]. He also says: “They rejoice in the life of this world, but the life of this world beside the Hereafter is only a brief enjoyment” [al-Raʿd 13:26]; and: “Say: The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for one who fears [Allah], and you will not be wronged by a date-thread” [al-Nisāʾ 4:77].

Relating the words of the believer among Pharaoh's people to his people, He says: “My people, follow me, and I will guide you to the path of right conduct. My people, this life of the world is only a passing enjoyment, and the Hereafter is the abode of permanence” [Ghāfir 40:38–39].
Allah has censured whoever seeks this world by his deeds, his striving and his intention; this was discussed above, in the commentary on the hadith “Deeds are only by intentions.”
The hadiths censuring this world and its worthlessness in Allah's sight are very many. In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Jābir:

The Prophet ﷺ passed through the market with people on either side of him, and came upon a dead kid with small ears. He picked it up, took hold of its ear and said: “Which of you would like to have this for a dirham?”
They said: We would not like to have it for anything; what would we do with it?
He said: “Would you like it to be yours?”
They said: By Allah, even if it were alive it would be defective,
because its ears are small; so how, when it is dead?
He said: “By Allah, this world is more worthless to Allah than this is to you.”
It also has, from al-Mustawrid al-Fihrī, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “This world compared with the Hereafter is only as if one of you put his finger in the sea; let him see what it comes back with.”

Al-Tirmidhī recorded, from the hadith of Sahl ibn Saʿd, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “If this world were worth a gnat's wing to Allah, He would not give a disbeliever a single drink of water from it.” He declared it authentic.

To be detached from a thing (zuhd) means to turn away from it because one regards it as little and contemptible and one's aspiration rises above it. One says shayʾ zahīd: a little, contemptible thing.

The Salaf and those after them spoke about the meaning of detachment from this world, and expressed it in various ways. A marfūʿ hadith (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ) has come on this, recorded by al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah through the narration of ʿAmr ibn Wāqid,
from Yūnus ibn Ḥalbas, from Abū Idrīs al-Khawlānī, from Abū Dharr, from the Prophet ﷺ,

who said: “Detachment from this world is not making the lawful unlawful or squandering wealth. Rather, detachment from this world is that you are not more confident in what is in your hand than in what is in the hand of Allah,
and that, when a misfortune strikes you, you desire its reward more than you would desire to have kept what you lost.”
Al-Tirmidhī said: Unusual (gharīb); we know it only by this route, and ʿAmr ibn Wāqid's hadith is munkar.

I say: The correct view is that it is mawqūf (stopping short of the Prophet ﷺ), as Imam Aḥmad reported it in Kitāb al-Zuhd: Zayd ibn Yaḥyā al-Dimashqī told us: Khālid ibn Ṣubayḥ told us: Yūnus ibn Ḥalbas told us: Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī said:

Detachment from this world is not making the lawful unlawful or squandering wealth. Detachment from this world is only that you are more confident in what is in the hand of Allah than in what is in your own hand, and that when you are struck by a misfortune you are more hopeful of its reward and of its being stored up for you than you would be of the thing itself, had it stayed with you.
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded it through the narration of Muḥammad ibn Muhājir, from Yūnus ibn Maysarah, who said: Detachment from this world is not making the lawful unlawful, nor squandering wealth;

rather, detachment from this world is that you are more confident in what is in the hand of Allah than in what is in your own hand; that your state when struck by a misfortune and your state when not struck by it are the same; and that the one who praises you and the one who censures you for keeping to the truth are the same to you.

So he explained detachment from this world by three things, all of them deeds of the heart, not of the limbs. That is why Abū Sulaymān used to say: Do not testify that anyone has zuhd, for zuhd is in the heart.

The first is that the servant is more confident in what is in the hand of Allah than in what is in his own hand. This arises from soundness and strength of certainty, for Allah has guaranteed His servants' provision and taken responsibility for it, as He says:

“There is no creature on earth but its provision rests on Allah” [Hūd 11:6]; and: “In heaven is your provision and what you are promised” [al-Dhāriyāt 51:22]; and: “So seek provision from Allah and worship Him” [al-ʿAnkabūt 29:17].
Al-Ḥasan said: It is a sign of the weakness of your certainty that you are more confident in what is in your hand than in what is in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
It is narrated that Ibn Masʿūd said: I am most hopeful of provision when they say: There is no flour in the house.
Masrūq said: My thoughts [of Allah] are best when the house servant says: There is not a qafīz of wheat or a dirham in the house.
Imam Aḥmad said: The happiest of my days is a day on which I wake up with nothing.
Abū Ḥāzim the ascetic was asked: What is your wealth?
He said: I have two kinds of wealth with which I do not fear poverty: trust in Allah, and despairing of what people possess.
He was asked: Do you not fear poverty?
He said: Should I fear poverty, when to my Master belongs all that is in the heavens and on earth, all that is between them and all that is beneath the soil?
A slip of paper was handed to ʿAlī ibn al-Muwaffaq. He read it, and in it was written: ʿAlī ibn al-Muwaffaq, do you fear poverty when I am your Lord?
Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said:
The root of zuhd is contentment with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
He also said: Being content with little (qunūʿ) is zuhd, and it is wealth.

Whoever realises certainty trusts Allah in all his affairs, is content with His disposal of him, and cuts himself off from attachment to created beings in hope and in fear, so that this prevents him from seeking this world by disliked means. Whoever is like that

is truly detached from this world, and is one of the richest of people, even if he has nothing of this world, as ʿAmmār said: Death suffices as an admonisher, certainty suffices as wealth, and worship suffices as an occupation.
Ibn Masʿūd said: Certainty is that you do not please people by angering Allah, do not praise anyone for Allah's provision, and do not blame anyone for what Allah has not given you;

for provision is not brought by the greed of the greedy, nor turned away by the dislike of one who dislikes it. Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, by His justice, knowledge and wisdom, has placed relief and joy in certainty and contentment, and placed worry and grief in doubt and discontent.

In a mursal hadith, the Prophet ﷺ used to supplicate with this supplication: “O Allah, I ask You for faith that touches my heart, and true certainty, so that I know that nothing will withhold from me provision You have allotted me; and make me content with the livelihood You have allotted me.”

ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī would not rise from his gathering until he had said: O Allah, grant us certainty from You, so that You make the misfortunes of this world easy for us, and so that we know that nothing will befall us but what You have written for us, and nothing of this provision will reach us but what You have allotted us.

We have narrated, from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās as marfūʿ: “Whoever would be glad to be the richest of people, let him be more confident in what is in the hand of Allah than in what is in his own hand.”

The second is that when the servant is struck by a misfortune in his worldly life — the loss of wealth, of a child or of something else — he desires its reward more than he desires that what he has lost of this world had stayed with him. This too arises from perfect certainty.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that the Prophet ﷺ used to say in his supplication: “O Allah, allot us such fear of You as will come between us and disobeying You, such obedience to You as will bring us to Your Paradise,

and such certainty as will make the misfortunes of this world easy for us.” This is one of the signs of detachment from this world and of little desire for it, as ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Misfortunes become easy for whoever is detached from this world.

The third is that the one who praises the servant and the one who censures him for keeping to the truth are the same to him. This is one of the signs of detachment from this world, of holding it in contempt and of little desire for it; for whoever holds this world in high regard loves praise and dislikes censure, and that may lead him to abandon much of the truth for fear of censure,

and to do much falsehood in hope of praise. When the one who praises him and the one who censures him for the truth are the same to him, this shows that created beings have lost their standing in his heart,
and that it is filled with love of the truth and of what pleases his Master, as Ibn Masʿūd said: Certainty is that you do not please people by angering Allah.
Allah has praised those who strive in the path of Allah and do not fear the blame of any blamer [al-Māʾidah 5:54].
Other expressions explaining detachment from this world have been narrated from the Salaf, all of which go back to what has been said, such as al-Ḥasan's saying:

The zāhid (one detached from the world) is one who, whenever he sees anyone, says: He is better than I am. This goes back to the point that the truly detached person is one who is detached from praise of himself and from exalting himself. That is why it is said:

Detachment from leadership is harder than detachment from gold and silver. Whoever expels from his heart love of leadership in this world and of rising above people in it is the truly detached one, and he is the one to whom the one who praises him and the one who censures him for the truth are the same.

Another is the saying of Wuhayb ibn al-Ward: Detachment from this world is that you do not grieve over what has passed you by of it and do not exult in what it has given you. Ibn al-Sammāk said: This is the zāhid who excels in his zuhd.
This goes back to its going and its coming, its increase and its decrease, being the same to the servant, which is like misfortune and its absence being the same, as was said above.
Someone — I think it was Imam Aḥmad — was asked about a man who has wealth: can he be a zāhid?
He said: If he does not exult when it increases or grieve when it decreases — or words to that effect.
Al-Zuhrī was asked about the zāhid and said: He is one whose patience the unlawful does not overcome, and whom the lawful does not distract from giving thanks. This is close to what came before it,

for its meaning is that when one who is detached from this world is able to get something unlawful from it, he patiently refrains from it and does not take it; and when he obtains something lawful from it, it does not distract him from giving thanks, but he thanks Allah for it.
Aḥmad ibn Abī al-Ḥawārī said: I said to Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah: Who is the one detached from this world?
He said: One who, when he is blessed, gives thanks, and when he is tried, is patient.
I said: Abū Muḥammad, he has been blessed and given thanks, tried and been patient, and has held on to the blessing; how can he be a zāhid?
He said: Be quiet! One whom blessings do not keep from giving thanks, nor trials from patience — that is the zāhid.
Rabīʿah said: The head of zuhd is to gather things rightfully and spend them rightfully.

Sufyān al-Thawrī said: Detachment from this world is keeping one's hopes short; it is not eating coarse food or wearing a woollen cloak. He also said: Among their supplications was: O Allah, make us detached from this world and give us plenty of it; do not withhold it from us and so make us desire it.
Imam Aḥmad likewise said: Detachment from this world is keeping one's hopes short; and he said once: Keeping one's hopes short and despairing of what people possess.

The reason for this is that short hopes bring about love of meeting Allah by leaving this world, while long hopes call for love of remaining in it. Whoever's hopes are short dislikes remaining in this world, and that is the utmost detachment from it and turning away from it.

Ibn ʿUyaynah cited as evidence for this view His words, Exalted is He: “Say: If the abode of the Hereafter with Allah is yours alone, to the exclusion of other people, then wish for death, if you are truthful” — up to His words: “And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life” [al-Baqarah 2:94–96].
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā reported, with his chain, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim, who said: A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: Messenger of Allah, who is the most detached of people?

He said: “One who does not forget the grave and decay, gives up the finest adornment of this world, prefers what lasts to what perishes, does not count tomorrow among his days, and counts himself among the dead.” This is mursal.

Many of the Salaf divided zuhd into categories. Some said: The best zuhd is detachment from shirk and from the worship of whatever is worshipped besides Allah; then detachment from everything unlawful, all sins;

then detachment from the lawful, which is the least of the categories of zuhd. The first two categories of this zuhd are both obligatory, while the third is not; for the greatest of obligations is detachment from shirk, and then from all sins.

Bakr al-Muzanī used to supplicate for his brothers: May Allah grant us and you the detachment of one who had the unlawful and sins within his reach in private, knew that Allah saw him, and so left them.
Ibn al-Mubārak said: Sallām ibn Abī Muṭīʿ said: Zuhd is of three kinds.
The first is to make one's deeds and words sincerely for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with nothing of them intended for this world.
The second is leaving what is not right and doing what is right.
The third is detachment from the lawful, which is voluntary; and it is the lowest of them.

This is close to what came before, except that he made the first degree of zuhd detachment from showing off (riyāʾ), which is contrary to sincerity in word and deed. Showing off is the lesser shirk, and what drives one to it is love of praise in this world and of standing high with its people, which is a kind of love of eminence and leadership in it.

Ibrāhīm ibn Adham said: Zuhd is of three kinds: obligatory zuhd, meritorious zuhd and zuhd for safety. The obligatory zuhd is detachment from the unlawful; the meritorious zuhd is detachment from the lawful; and the zuhd for safety is detachment from doubtful things (shubuhāt).
People have differed over whether someone who is detached from the unlawful alone, but not from the surplus of permissible things, deserves the name zāhid or not,
holding two views. The first is that this is enough for him to deserve the name; this view has been given above from al-Zuhrī, Ibn ʿUyaynah and others.

The second is that he does not deserve the name without detachment from the surplus of the permissible. This is the view of a group of those who know Allah (al-ʿārifūn) and others, so much so that some of them said: There is no zuhd today, because the purely permissible is no longer to be found. This is the view of Yūsuf ibn Asbāṭ and others, but it is open to question.
Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd used to say: What is this world worth, that one who is detached from it should be praised?

Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī said: In Iraq they have given us differing views on zuhd. Some said zuhd lies in giving up meeting people; some said, in giving up appetites; and some said, in giving up eating one's fill.

Their words are close to one another. He said: My own view is that zuhd lies in giving up whatever distracts you from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. What Abū Sulaymān said is good, and it brings together all the meanings, categories and kinds of zuhd.

Know that the censure of this world in the Book and the Sunnah does not refer to its time, the night and day that follow each other until the Day of Resurrection; for Allah has made them succeed one another for whoever wishes to take heed or wishes to give thanks [al-Furqān 25:62].

It is narrated that ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) said: This night and day are two treasuries, so look at what you put in them. He used to say: Use the night for what it was created for, and the day for what it was created for.
Mujāhid said: There is no day but it says: Son of Ādam, I have come in to you today, and I will never return to you after today; so look at what you do in me. When it has ended,
it is folded up and sealed, and it is not unsealed until Allah opens it on the Day of Resurrection; and every night says the same. One of the Salaf recited:
This world is only a road / to Paradise or to the Fire;
the nights are man's place of trade, / and the days are the market.

Nor does the censure refer to the place of this world, the earth which Allah has made a bed and a dwelling for the children of Ādam; nor to the mountains, seas, rivers and minerals He has placed in it; nor to the trees and crops He has made to grow in it;
nor to the animals and other things He has spread in it. All of that is part of Allah's blessing to His servants, for the benefits they have in it,

and for the lessons they draw from it and the evidence it gives them of the oneness, power and greatness of its Maker. The censure refers only to the actions of the children of Ādam that take place in this world,

because most of them are not done in a way that ends well; rather, they are done in a way that ends in harm, or in no benefit, as the Mighty and Majestic says: “Know that the life of this world is only play and amusement, adornment, boasting among yourselves and rivalry in wealth and children” [al-Ḥadīd 57:20].
The children of Ādam in this world are divided into two groups.

The first are those who deny that the servants have any abode of reward and punishment after this world. They are the ones of whom Allah says: “Those who do not hope to meet Us, are content with the life of this world and at ease in it, and those who are heedless of Our signs — their refuge is the Fire, for what they used to earn” [Yūnus 10:7–8].

Their concern is to enjoy this world and snatch its pleasures before death, as the Exalted says: “Those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, and the Fire will be their dwelling” [Muḥammad 47:12].
Some of these used to enjoin detachment from this world,

because they held that taking much of it brings worry and distress, and said: The more one is attached to it, the more the soul suffers at parting from it at death. That was the extent of their detachment from this world.

The second group are those who affirm an abode of reward and punishment after death; they are those who adhere to the laws brought by the messengers. They are divided into three categories: one who wrongs himself, one who takes a middle course, and one who is foremost in good deeds by Allah's leave [Fāṭir 35:32].

Those who wrong themselves are the majority of them. Most of them stop at the glitter and adornment of this world, taking it from other than its proper source and using it in other than its proper way.

This world has become their greatest concern: for it they grow angry and with it they are pleased; for it they befriend and over it they show enmity. These are the people of play, amusement, adornment, boasting and rivalry in increase.

None of them has understood the purpose of this world, nor that it is a stopping place on a journey, from which one takes provision for the abode of residence after it; and even if one of them believes in that in a general way,
he does not know it in detail, nor has he tasted what those who know Allah taste in this world, which is a foretaste of what has been stored up for them in the Hereafter.

The one who takes a middle course takes this world by its permissible means and fulfils its obligations, but keeps for himself what is beyond the obligatory, using it to enjoy the appetites of this world more amply.

There is disagreement, as mentioned above, over whether these fall under the name of detachment from this world. They are not punished for that, except that their degrees in the Hereafter are reduced in proportion to their indulgence in this world.
Ibn ʿUmar said: A servant gets nothing of this world but it reduces his degrees with Allah, even if he is honoured by Him. Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded it with a sound chain.
It has been narrated as marfūʿ from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, with a chain open to question.

Imam Aḥmad reported in Kitāb al-Zuhd, with his chain, that a man went in to Muʿāwiyah, who gave him clothes. He came out and passed by Abū Masʿūd al-Anṣārī and another of the Companions. One of them said to him: Take it out of your good deeds; and the other said: Out of your good things.

With his chain, from ʿUmar, who said: Were it not that my good deeds would be reduced, I would join you in your soft living; but I have heard Allah reproach a people, saying: “You used up your good things in your worldly life” [al-Aḥqāf 46:20].
Al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said: If you wish, take little of this world; and if you wish, take much of it; for you are only taking from your own purse.

This is borne out by the fact that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has forbidden His servants some of the surplus pleasures, adornment and splendour of this world, since they had no need of them, and has stored them up for them with Him in the Hereafter. This is alluded to in His words, the Mighty and Majestic:

“Were it not that mankind would become a single community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses, and stairways…” — up to His words: “Yet all that is only the enjoyment of the life of this world, and the Hereafter with your Lord is for the God-fearing” [al-Zukhruf 43:33–35].
It is authentically reported that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever wears silk in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter,” and “Whoever drinks wine in this world will not drink it in the Hereafter.”
He also said: “Do not wear silk or brocade, and do not drink from vessels of gold and silver or eat from plates made of them; for they are theirs in this world and yours in the Hereafter.”

Wahb said: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said to Mūsā (peace be upon him): I keep My friends away from the comfort and ease of this world, as a caring shepherd keeps his camels away from places where mange is caught.
That is not because they are lowly in My sight, but so that they may receive their full share of My honour, safe and complete, untouched by this world.
This is borne out by what al-Tirmidhī recorded from Qatādah ibn al-Nuʿmān, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “When Allah loves a servant, He protects him from this world,

as one of you keeps water from his sick one.” Al-Ḥākim recorded it with the wording: “Allah protects His servant from this world while He loves him, as you keep food and drink from your sick ones, fearing for them.”
In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr, the Prophet ﷺ said: “This world is the believer's prison and the disbeliever's paradise.”

As for one who is foremost in good deeds by Allah's leave, they are those who have understood the purpose of this world and acted accordingly. They knew that Allah has settled His servants in this abode only to test them, which of them is best in deed,

as He says: “It is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days — and His Throne was upon the water — to test you, which of you is best in deed” [Hūd 11:7]; and: “who created death and life to test you, which of you is best in deed” [al-Mulk 67:2].

One of the Salaf said: [That is:] which of them is most detached from this world and most desirous of the Hereafter. He has made the splendour and freshness of this world a trial, to see which of them will stop at it and rely on it,

and which will not, as the Exalted says: “We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it, to test them, which of them is best in deed” [al-Kahf 18:7]. Then He made clear that it would come to an end and run out, saying: “And We shall make what is on it a barren plain” [al-Kahf 18:8].

When they understood that this is the purpose of this world, they made it their concern to take provision from it for the Hereafter, which is the abode of permanence, and contented themselves with as much of this world as a traveller contents himself with on his journey,

as the Prophet ﷺ used to say: “What have I to do with this world? My likeness and that of this world is only that of a rider who took a midday rest in the shade of a tree, and then went on and left it.”
He ﷺ counselled a number of the Companions that each one's sufficiency from this world should be like a rider's provisions; among them were Salmān, Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ,
Abū Dharr and ʿĀʾishah. And he counselled Ibn ʿUmar to be in this world as though he were a stranger or a wayfarer, and to count himself among the people of the graves.
The people of this degree are of two kinds. Some limit themselves to as much of this world as keeps them alive and no more; this is the state of many of the ascetics.
Others sometimes allow themselves some of its permissible pleasures,

so that the soul may be strengthened by that and become eager for work, as is narrated of the Prophet ﷺ that he said: “Of your world, women and perfume have been made dear to me, and the delight of my eye has been placed in prayer.” Imam Aḥmad and al-Nasāʾī recorded it from the hadith of Anas.
Imam Aḥmad recorded, from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah, who said: Of this world the Messenger of Allah ﷺ loved women, perfume and food. He had his share of women and perfume, but not of food.

Wahb said: It is written in the wisdom of the family of Dāwūd (peace be upon him): The intelligent man should not neglect four hours: an hour in which he calls himself to account, an hour in which he converses intimately with his Lord, an hour in which he meets his brothers who tell him of his faults

and are truthful with him about himself, and an hour in which he leaves himself free to enjoy its pleasures in what is lawful and seemly. For this hour is a help towards those hours, an extra provision and a refreshing of the hearts — that is, giving them rest.

Whenever the believer intends, by enjoying his permissible appetites, to gain strength for obedience, his appetites become for him an act of obedience for which he is rewarded, as Muʿādh ibn Jabal said:

I hope for reward for my sleep as I hope for reward for my standing [in prayer]. He meant that by his sleep he intended to gain strength for standing in prayer at the end of the night, so he hoped for the reward of his sleep as he hoped for the reward of his standing.

When some of them had some of their permissible pleasures, they would share them with their brothers. So it is narrated of Ibn al-Mubārak that when he desired something, he would not eat it until one of his companions desired it, and then he would eat it with them; and when he desired something, he would invite a guest to eat it with him.
It used to be related of al-Awzāʿī that he said: There are three who will have no reckoning for their food:
the one who eats the pre-dawn meal (saḥūr), the fasting person when he breaks his fast, and [the one who eats] the food of a guest.

Al-Ḥasan said: It is not part of your love of this world to seek what puts you right in it; and it is part of your detachment from it to give up a need when giving it up serves you as well as meeting it. When a person loves this world and is delighted by it, fear of the Hereafter leaves his heart.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: The enjoyment of delusion is whatever distracts you from seeking the Hereafter; whatever does not distract you is not the enjoyment of delusion, but an enjoyment that brings you to something better than it.
Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh al-Rāzī said: How could I not love a world in which a sustenance has been decreed for me, by which I gain a life, by which I attain obedience, by which I reach the Hereafter?
Abū Ṣafwān al-Ruʿaynī — who was one of those who know Allah — was asked: What is the world that Allah has censured in the Qurʾān, which the intelligent person should avoid?
He said: Everything you obtain in this world by which you seek this world is censured, and everything you obtain in it by which you seek the Hereafter is not part of it.

Al-Ḥasan said: What an excellent abode this world was for the believer! For he did a little work and took from it his provision for Paradise. And what an evil abode it was for the disbeliever and the hypocrite! For he squandered his nights, and his provision from it was for the Fire.

Ayfaʿ ibn ʿAbd al-Kalāʿī said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “When the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire the Fire, Allah will say: People of Paradise, how many years did you remain on earth?

They will say: We remained a day or part of a day. He will say: How well you traded in a day or part of a day: My mercy, My good pleasure and My Paradise. Remain in it, abiding for ever. Then He will say to the people of the Fire: How many years did you remain on earth?
They will say: We remained a day or part of a day. He will say: How badly you traded in a day or part of a day: My anger, disobedience to Me and My Fire. Remain in it, abiding for ever.”

Al-Ḥākim recorded, from the hadith of ʿAbd al-Jabbār ibn Wahb: Saʿd ibn Ṭāriq informed us, from his father, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “What an excellent abode this world is for one who takes provision from it for his Hereafter until he pleases his Lord; and what an evil abode for one whom it turns away from his Hereafter

and keeps from his Lord's good pleasure. When the servant says, ‘May Allah make this world ugly!’, the world says: ‘May Allah make ugly whichever of us is more disobedient to his Lord!’” He said: Its chain is authentic.
Al-ʿUqaylī recorded it and said: ʿAbd al-Jabbār ibn Wahb is unknown, and his hadith is not preserved. He said: These words are narrated from ʿAlī as his own.

As for ʿAlī's words, Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded them from him with a chain open to question: ʿAlī heard a man reviling this world and said: It is an abode of truthfulness for whoever is truthful with it, an abode of well-being for whoever understands it, an abode of wealth for whoever takes provision from it; the place of prostration of Allah's beloved ones, the place where His revelation descends,

the place of prayer of His angels and the place of trade of His friends, who earned mercy in it and gained Paradise as their profit in it. Who then censures this world, when it has announced its departure, proclaimed its faults,

and described itself and its people, showing by its affliction a likeness of the affliction [to come], and by its joy arousing longing for the joy [to come]? Some censured it at the moment of regret, while others praised it: it spoke to them and they believed, it reminded them and they took heed.
You who are deluded by this world, beguiled by its beguilement, when did this world ever give you cause to blame it?
Or rather, when did it deceive you?
With the resting places of your fathers in the dust?
Or with the places where your mothers fell into decay?

How many a sick man have you turned with your palms and nursed with your hands, seeking a cure for him and asking the physicians on his behalf, yet you did not attain your need and were not granted your request! By his death this world has shown you a likeness of your own death tomorrow, when your weeping will not avail you and your loved ones will not benefit you.

So the Commander of the Believers (may Allah be pleased with him) made clear that this world is not to be censured absolutely, and that it is praiseworthy for whoever takes righteous deeds from it as provision;

that in it are the places of prostration of the prophets and the place where revelation descends; and that it is the abode of trade for the believers, who earned mercy in it and gained Paradise through it as their profit. So it is an excellent abode for whoever has this description.

As for what is said about its deluding and deceiving, it calls out with its admonitions and gives sincere counsel by its lessons, and it shows its faults by what it lets its people see of the places where the perishing fall, and of the turning of states from health to sickness,

from youth to old age, from wealth to poverty and from might to abasement. But the one who loves it has been deafened and blinded by his love of it, so that he does not hear its call, as it has been said:
This world has proclaimed its own nature, / if only there were someone in the world to hear:
How many who trusted in life I have brought to an end, / and how many a hoarder whose hoard I have scattered!
Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh said: If creatures heard the sound of the lamentation over this world, in the unseen, from the tongues of extinction, their hearts would fall from them in grief.

One of the sages said: This world is a set of parables that the days strike for mankind; the knowledge that time teaches needs no interpreter; through love of this world the ears of the hearts have been deafened to admonitions; and how hard the driver urges us on, if only creatures perceived it!
Those who are detached from the surplus of this world are of several kinds. Some obtain it and hold on to it, seeking nearness to Allah by it, as many of the Companions and others did.
Abū Sulaymān said: ʿUthmān and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf were two of Allah's treasurers on His earth, spending in obedience to Him, and their dealing with Allah was with their hearts.

Others put it out of their hands and do not hold on to it. These are of two types: some put it out by choice and willingly, and some put it out though their souls resist, struggling against them to do it.

There is disagreement over which of the two is better. Ibn al-Sammāk and al-Junayd said: The first is better, because his soul has truly attained the station of generosity and zuhd. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: The second is better,
because he has both effort and struggle to his credit.
There is also something in the words of Imam Aḥmad that indicates this.
Others obtain nothing of the surplus, and are detached from acquiring it, whether they are able to acquire it or not. The first [kind] is better than this,
and that is why many of the Salaf said that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was more detached than Uways and those like him; so said Abū Sulaymān and others.
Mālik ibn Dīnār used to say: People say Mālik is a zāhid; the zāhid is only ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.

The scholars have differed over which is better: one who seeks this world from what is lawful in order to keep ties with his kin and send something ahead for himself, or one who leaves it and does not seek it at all.

One group, among them al-Ḥasan and others, preferred the one who leaves it and keeps away from it; another group, among them al-Nakhaʿī and others, preferred the one who seeks it in that way; and something like this has also been narrated from al-Ḥasan.

Those who are detached from this world in their hearts look at it from different points of view, each contemplating something in particular. Some see how much toil there is in striving to acquire it, so they are detached from it in order to give themselves rest.
Al-Ḥasan said: Detachment from this world gives rest to the heart and the body.
Some fear that their share of the Hereafter will be reduced by taking the surplus of this world.
Some fear the long reckoning for it. One of them said: Whoever asks Allah for this world is only asking for a long standing at the reckoning.
Some see how many faults this world has, how quickly it changes and passes away, and how the base crowd one in seeking it. Thus one of them was asked: What made you detached from this world?
He said: Its little loyalty, its great harshness and the baseness of its partners.

Some look at the worthlessness of this world in Allah's sight and find it repugnant, as al-Fuḍayl said: If the whole of this world were offered to me lawfully, with no reckoning for it in the Hereafter, I would still find it as repugnant as a man finds a carcass he passes, lest it touch his garment.
Some fear that it will distract them from preparing for the Hereafter and taking provision for it.
Al-Ḥasan said: One of them would live his whole life in hardship and great strain, with lawful wealth beside him, and would be told: Will you not go to this and take some of it?
And he would say: No, by Allah, I will not. I fear that if I go to it and take some of it, it will be the ruin of my heart and my deeds.

Wealth was sent to ʿUmar ibn al-Munkadir, and he wept, weeping hard, and said: I feared that this world would overcome my heart and leave no share in it for the Hereafter; that is what made me weep. Then he gave orders for it, and it was given in charity to the poor of Madīnah.

The elect among these fear being distracted by it from Allah, as Rābiʿah said: I would not like to have the whole of this world, from its beginning to its end, lawfully, and spend it in the path of Allah, if it distracted me from Allah for the blink of an eye.
Abū Sulaymān said: Zuhd is giving up whatever distracts from Allah.
He also said: Whatever distracts you from Allah — family, wealth or children — is an ill omen for you.

He also said: The people of detachment from this world are of two levels. Some are detached from this world, yet the refreshment of the Hereafter is not opened to them in it; and some, when they become detached from it, have the refreshment of the Hereafter opened to them in it, so that nothing is dearer to them than remaining, in order to obey Allah.
He also said: The zāhid is not one who has thrown off the worries of this world and rested from them; the zāhid is only one who is detached from this world and toils in it for the Hereafter.
So detachment from this world means emptying the heart of preoccupation with it,
so that it is free to seek Allah, to know Him, to draw near to Him, to find intimacy with Him and to long to meet Him. These things are not part of this world, as the Prophet ﷺ used to say:
“Of your world, women and perfume have been made dear to me, and the delight of my eye has been placed in prayer”; he did not count prayer among the things of this world that were made dear to him.

So it is in the Musnad and al-Nasāʾī; I think that elsewhere it occurs as “Of your world three things have been made dear to me,” which counts prayer as part of this world. Supporting this is the hadith:

“This world is cursed, and cursed is what is in it, except the remembrance of Allah and what goes with it, or a scholar or a student.” Ibn Mājah and al-Tirmidhī recorded it from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah as marfūʿ, and al-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan.
Something similar has been narrated by other routes, both mursal and connected.
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded, from the hadith of Abū al-Dardāʾ as marfūʿ: “This world is cursed, and cursed is what is in it, except what is sought by it for the Face of Allah.”
Ibn Abī al-Dunyā recorded it as mawqūf,

and he also recorded, through the narration of Shahr ibn Ḥawshab, from ʿUbādah — I think he raised it to the Prophet ﷺ — that he said: “This world will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said: Pick out from it whatever was for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and throw the rest into the Fire.”
So this world and everything in it is cursed, that is, kept far from Allah,

because it distracts from Him — except beneficial knowledge that leads to Allah, to knowing Him and to seeking His nearness and good pleasure, and the remembrance of Allah and what goes with it of things that bring one near to Allah. This is what this world is for,

for Allah has commanded His servants only to fear Him and obey Him, and that necessarily entails remembering Him constantly, as Ibn Masʿūd said: To fear Allah as He truly deserves to be feared is that He be remembered and not forgotten.
Allah prescribed keeping up the prayer only for His remembrance, and likewise the Ḥajj and circumambulation.

The best of the people of worship are those who remember Allah most in it. None of this belongs to the censured world; rather, it is the purpose for which this world and its people were brought into being, as the Exalted says: “I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me” [al-Dhāriyāt 51:56].

Groups of jurists and Sufis have thought that these acts of worship found in this world are better than the bliss found in Paradise. They said: That is because the bliss of Paradise is the servant's right, while the acts of worship in this world are the Lord's right,

and the Lord's right is better than the servant's portion. This is a mistake. Their mistake is reinforced by what many of the exegetes say about His words, “Whoever brings a good deed will have better than it” [al-Naml 27:89; al-Qaṣaṣ 28:84]: they said that the good deed is lā ilāha illā Allāh, and nothing is better than it.
But the phrase is to be read with its words rearranged, and what is meant is: he will have good from it, that is, he will have good because of it and for its sake.
The correct position is to state without qualification what the texts of the Book and the Sunnah have brought: that the Hereafter is better than this first life, without qualification.

In al-Ḥākim's Ṣaḥīḥ, from al-Mustawrid ibn Shaddād, who said: We were with the Prophet ﷺ, and they discussed this world and the Hereafter. Some of them said: This world is only a means of reaching the Hereafter; in it are deeds, in it is prayer, in it is zakāh.

Another group of them said: The Hereafter has Paradise in it; and they said what Allah willed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “This world compared with the Hereafter is only as if one of you walked to the sea
and put his finger in it; whatever comes out with it is this world.” This is an explicit text preferring the Hereafter over this world and the deeds that are in it.

The reason for this is that the perfection of this world lies only in knowledge and action, and knowledge, which is the aim of the deeds, is multiplied in the Hereafter beyond any comparison with what is in this world.

For the root of knowledge is knowing Allah, His names and His attributes; and in the Hereafter the veil is lifted, report becomes sight, knowledge of certainty becomes the eye of certainty, and knowing Allah becomes seeing Him and beholding Him. Where is this compared with what is in this world?
As for the bodily deeds, they have two purposes in this world.
The first is the occupation of the limbs in obedience and their exertion in worship.
The second is the connection of the hearts with Allah and their illumination by His remembrance.

The first has been lifted from the people of Paradise. That is why it is narrated that when they move to prostrate to Allah as He manifests Himself to them, they will be told: Raise your heads, for you are not in an abode of striving.

As for the second purpose, the people of Paradise attain it in the most perfect and complete way. What their hearts attained in this world of the subtleties of nearness, intimacy and connection bears no comparison with what they will behold openly in the Hereafter,
where their hearts, eyes and ears will delight in Allah's nearness, in seeing Him and in hearing His speech, especially at the times of the prayers of this world,
such as Fridays and the Eids; and for those brought near among them this will happen twice every day, morning and evening, at the time of the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer.
That is why, when the Prophet ﷺ mentioned that the people of Paradise will see their Lord, he urged straight afterwards that the afternoon prayer and the dawn prayer be guarded,

because the time of these two prayers is a time when the elect of the people of Paradise see their Lord and visit Him. Likewise the bliss of remembrance and of reciting the Qurʾān will never be cut off from them: they will be inspired with glorification as they are inspired with breath.

Ibn ʿUyaynah said: Lā ilāha illā Allāh is to the people of Paradise like cold water to the people of this world. How far is the delight of remembrance for those who know Allah in this world from their delight in it in Paradise!

It is clear from this that His words, “Whoever brings a good deed will have better than it,” are to be taken in their apparent sense; for the reward of the word of tawḥīd in this world is that the one who says it comes to say it in Paradise in the manner peculiar to the people of Paradise.

In any case, what the people of Paradise attain of the details of knowledge of Allah, His names, attributes and acts, and of His nearness, of beholding Him and of the delight of His remembrance, is something whose essence cannot be expressed in this world,

because its people have not grasped it as it truly is. Rather, it is something no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that has never occurred to any human heart. We ask Allah the Exalted not to deprive us of the best of what He has because of the worst of what we have, by His favour, generosity and mercy. Āmīn.

Let us return to the explanation of the hadith, “Be detached from this world and Allah will love you.” This hadith shows that Allah loves those who are detached from this world. One of the Salaf said:

The disciples said to ʿĪsā (peace be upon him): Spirit of Allah, teach us a single deed for which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will love us. He said: Hate this world, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will love you.

Allah the Exalted has censured those who love this world and prefer it to the Hereafter, as He says: “No! Rather, you love the fleeting [life] and leave the Hereafter” [al-Qiyāmah 75:20–21]; and: “And you love wealth with an excessive love” [al-Fajr 89:20];

and: “And indeed he is intense in his love of good [things]” [al-ʿĀdiyāt 100:8], meaning love of wealth. His censure of whoever loves this world shows that He praises whoever does not love it but rejects and leaves it.

In the Musnad and Ṣaḥīḥ Ibn Ḥibbān, from Abū Mūsā, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever loves his world harms his Hereafter, and whoever loves his Hereafter harms his world; so prefer what lasts to what perishes.”
In the Musnad and the Sunan of Ibn Mājah, from Zayd ibn Thābit, the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever has this world as his concern, Allah scatters his affairs,

places his poverty between his eyes, and nothing of this world comes to him but what has been written for him. Whoever has the Hereafter as his intention, Allah gathers his affairs for him, places his wealth in his heart, and this world comes to him in spite of itself.”
Al-Tirmidhī recorded something with this meaning from the hadith of Anas as marfūʿ.
Among the sayings of Jundab ibn ʿAbdullāh the Companion: Love of this world is the head of every sin. It has also been narrated as marfūʿ, and from al-Ḥasan in mursal form.
Al-Ḥasan said: When a person loves this world and is delighted by it, love of the Hereafter leaves his heart.
ʿAwn ibn ʿAbdullāh said: This world and the Hereafter in the heart are like the two pans of a balance: as much as one goes down, the other goes up.
Wahb said: This world and the Hereafter are only like a man with two wives: if he pleases one, he angers the other.

In any case, detachment from this world is the hallmark of Allah's prophets, His friends and His beloved ones. ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ said: How far your way is from the way of your Prophet ﷺ! He was the most detached of people from this world, and you are the most desirous of people for it. Imam Aḥmad recorded it.
Ibn Masʿūd said to his companions: You fast, pray and strive in jihād more than the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ did, yet they were better than you. They said: How is that?
He said: They were more detached from this world than you, and more desirous of the Hereafter.
Abū al-Dardāʾ said: If you swore to me about a man that he was the most detached of you, I would swear to you that he was the best of you.
It is narrated that al-Ḥasan said: They said: Messenger of Allah, who is the best of us?
He said: “The most detached of you from this world and the most desirous of you for the Hereafter.” Discussion of this subject would be very long;
what we have pointed to will suffice, if Allah the Exalted wills.
The second counsel is detachment from what people possess, and that it brings about people's love.
It is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ counselled a man, saying: “Despair of what people possess, and you will be rich.” Al-Ṭabarānī and others recorded it.
It is narrated, from the hadith of Sahl ibn Saʿd as marfūʿ: “The believer's honour is his standing [in prayer] at night, and his might is his independence of people.”

Al-Ḥasan said: You will remain honoured by people — or, people will continue to honour you — so long as you do not reach for what is in their hands. When you do that, they will think little of you, dislike your talk and hate you.
Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī said: A man does not become noble until he has two traits: restraint from what people possess, and overlooking what comes from them.
ʿUmar used to say in his sermon from the pulpit: Greed is poverty and despair is wealth; when a person despairs of a thing, he can do without it.
It is narrated that ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām met Kaʿb al-Aḥbār in ʿUmar's presence and said: Kaʿb, who are the masters of knowledge?
He said: Those who act on it. He said: Then what takes knowledge away from the hearts of the scholars after they have memorised and understood it?
He said: Greed, the soul's avidity and seeking one's needs from people take it away. He said: You are right.
The hadiths from the Prophet ﷺ commanding people to refrain from asking others and to be independent of them are numerous. People dislike and hate whoever asks them for what is in their hands,
because wealth is beloved to the souls of the children of Ādam, and they dislike whoever asks them for what they love.

As for one who regards the asker as having done him a favour, and holds that even if he gave him all his property he would not have repaid him for asking him and humbling himself before him, or who used to say to his family:

Your clothes look better on others than on you, and your mounts look better under others than under you — this is very rare in the nature of the children of Ādam, and that carpet was rolled up long ages ago.

As for one who is detached from what people possess and refrains from it, they love and honour him for it, and by it he becomes their master. Thus a Bedouin asked the people of al-Baṣrah: Who is the master of the people of this town?
They said: Al-Ḥasan. He said: By what did he become their master?
They said: People needed his knowledge, while he had no need of their worldly goods. How fine is the saying of one of the Salaf describing this world and its people:
It is nothing but a rotting carcass, / with dogs upon it intent on dragging it off;
if you keep away from it, you are at peace with its people, / and if you drag at it, its dogs will fight you for it.
